class_criteria.high: IARC Group 1 or 2A with a dietary exposure route; or EFSA has withdrawn or negated a safety conclusion; or EFSA’s own exposure assessment finds a child age group exceeding the ADI at mean intake; or the substance is banned or formally being phased out for food use by the EU, by the US FDA, or under a US state law.
class_criteria.mid: IARC Group 2B; or an EFSA re-evaluation that flagged genotoxicity data gaps, found safety could not be assessed on the available data, or cut the ADI citing child exposure; or an EU harmonised classification of the substance as a reproductive or developmental hazard; or an EU withdrawal of one authorised food use while others remain; or an OEHHA/Proposition 65 listing; or membership of the Southampton-six colourants.
class_criteria.low: A credible adverse or precautionary signal that stops short of every Moderate and High criterion: peer-reviewed adverse findings not yet reflected in regulatory status, an exposure exceedance confined to high-percentile or single-event estimates, or a precautionary regulatory step short of those criteria — a reduced ADI, a data limitation noted without an adverse conclusion, a narrowed or conditioned authorisation, or a child-focused assessment or school-food law that covers the additive as part of a class.
class_criteria.none: Clean current EFSA and FDA status. These rows exist so that an unfamiliar additive is never treated as a bad one: a missing row costs a product nothing, and a clean row says so with citations.

citations.finding: Both school-meal statutes name azodicarbonamide — the sub-form a bare en:e927 tag overwhelmingly resolves to — so the parent carries the same child flag as en:e927a; see that row for the full citation.
citations.simple: Texas and Louisiana ban the main form of this in school meals, so it is marked for children.

citations.ref: Canas BJ et al., Food Additives and Contaminants 1997;14(1) (PMID 9059587); Dennis MJ et al., Food Additives and Contaminants 1997;14(1) (PMID 9059588)
citations.finding: At the US-permitted 45 mg/kg flour treatment level, azodicarbonamide led to significant increases in ethyl carbamate concentrations in both bread and toast, on the order of 1–3 µg/kg. Ethyl carbamate is IARC Group 2A. This is the strongest primary signal behind the low class: a dietary formation route at the permitted use level with no concluded regulatory assessment.
citations.simple: When used in bread at the allowed level, it can create tiny amounts of a chemical that may cause cancer.

citations.ref: Becalski A et al., J Agric Food Chem 2004, 10.1021/jf0495385; Noonan GO et al., J Agric Food Chem 2005, 10.1021/jf050480j (PMID 15941299); Noonan GO et al., J Agric Food Chem 2008 (PMID 18303820)
citations.finding: Semicarbazide forms in ADA-treated flour only on baking, via a biurea intermediate; free semicarbazide was measured at 10–1,200 µg/kg (mean ~260 µg/kg) in commercial US breads. Context rather than the basis of the class: both EFSA (2005) and FDA (2016) have since assessed dietary semicarbazide and found no concern.
citations.simple: Baking can create a chemical from this in bread, but experts later found no health worry about it.
citations.source_title: Semicarbazide Formation in Azodicarbonamide-Treated Flour:  A Model Study
citations.source_journal: Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry

citations.ref: EFSA AFC Panel statement on semicarbazide, 1 July 2005 (efsa.europa.eu/en/press/news/afc050701)
citations.finding: New in-vivo data showed a lack of genotoxic activity; the Panel judged carcinogenicity 'not of concern for human health' at reported semicarbazide levels, while reconfirming infant food as the most important exposure source via packaging gaskets — a route Commission Directive 2004/1/EC closed from August 2005.
citations.simple: Experts found a related chemical was not harmful to the body's cells and was not a worry for health.

citations.ref: 21 CFR 172.806 and 21 CFR 137.105 (eCFR); FDA, 'Azodicarbonamide (ADA) — Questions and Answers' (fda.gov), including the 2016 semicarbazide exposure assessment presented at the ACS 251st National Meeting
citations.finding: Azodicarbonamide is permitted in the US as an ageing/bleaching ingredient in cereal flour and as a dough conditioner at up to 45 ppm. FDA's 2016 exposure assessment of semicarbazide from bread — covering the general population and children aged 2–5, the group expected to have the highest exposure per body weight — recommended no dietary change and reaffirmed ADA as safe at the permitted level.
citations.simple: The US still counts this as safe in flour at the allowed level, and young children's bread intake was checked.

citations.ref: FDA Request for Information: Azodicarbonamide (ADA), 91 FR 27060, docket FDA-2026-N-4126 (published 2026-05-13; comment period closed 2026-07-13); FDA news release 'FDA finalizes food chemical safety post-market assessment program, launches reassessment of BHT and ADA' (2026-05-12)
citations.finding: FDA selected azodicarbonamide as one of the first two chemicals in its post-market reassessment programme, and the Request for Information explicitly seeks data on residual levels of ADA's decomposition products, including semicarbazide and ethyl carbamate. Not a ban, a phase-out or a safety finding — but the US status is under active review rather than settled, which is why this row sits at low rather than none.
citations.simple: The US is reviewing this again, which is not a ban, but its status is not settled.

citations.ref: Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 Annex II (EU Union list of food additives); Commission Directive 2004/1/EC (ADC prohibited as a blowing agent in food-contact plastics from 2 Aug 2005)
citations.finding: Azodicarbonamide has no entry in the EU list of permitted food additives — non-authorisation, not a ban — and its food-contact use was separately prohibited in 2005. Neither is a withdrawal of an authorised food use, so no high trigger fires.
citations.simple: The EU does not allow this in food, and it is also banned from some food packaging.

citations.ref: US-TX: S.B. 314 (89R, signed 2025-05-27; free and reduced-price school-meal contracts from 2026-09-01); US-LA: S.B. 14 / Act 463 (signed June 2025; school food from the 2028–29 school year)
citations.finding: Both statutes name azodicarbonamide among the ingredients barred from school meals. Child-specific regulatory language — the basis for higher-concern-for-young-children flag, exactly as on E 132, E 133 and E 143. School statutes are not Red-3-class food bans, so they do not raise the class.
citations.simple: Texas and Louisiana ban this in school meals, so it is marked as a bigger worry for young children.

citations.ref: Commission Regulation (EU) No 1129/2011 (establishing Annex II Part B to Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008); Commission Regulation (EU) No 231/2012, specifications for E 927b CARBAMIDE
citations.finding: VERIFIED in the primary text: 'E 927b Carbamide' is listed in Annex II Part B among additives other than colours and sweeteners — the Union positive list — and Reg 231/2012 gives it full identity and purity specifications (synonym urea, assay not less than 99.0%). The permitted use is chewing gum with no added sugar at a maximum of 30,000 mg/kg; the Part B listing was quoted directly, while the 30,000 mg/kg level is corroborated by secondary additive databases and by JECFA's 3% figure rather than quoted from the truncated consolidated Part E text.
citations.simple: The EU allows this only in sugar-free chewing gum, and it has clear rules about what it must contain.

citations.ref: JECFA evaluations — urea/carbamide (WHO/FAO JECFA database, chemical 2177; 41st meeting, 1993)
citations.finding: 'Use at levels of up to 3% in chewing-gum not of toxicological concern.' This is a positive assessment at the same level the EU permits — the classification rests on an affirmative clean finding, not on an absence of evidence.
citations.simple: Experts found that this is safe in chewing gum at the amount the EU allows.

citations.ref: 10.2903/j.efsa.2023.8112 (EFSA 2023 peer review of the pesticide risk assessment for urea) and 10.2903/j.efsa.2011.2071 (EFSA NDA Panel 2011, carbamide chewing gum and plaque acid neutralisation, claim ID 1153)
citations.finding: Supportive, not load-bearing. The 2023 pesticide peer review notes urea's historical safe use as food additive E 927b; the 2011 NDA opinion assessed a positive health claim for carbamide chewing gum without raising a safety concern. No EFSA re-evaluation of E 927b as a food additive has been published as of 2026-08.
citations.simple: Experts have long seen this used safely in food, and they did not raise any health worry.
citations.source_title: Peer review of the pesticide risk assessment of the active substance urea

citations.ref: FDA Substances Added to Food inventory — calcium peroxide (hfpappexternal.fda.gov/scripts/fdcc/index.cfm?set=FoodSubstances&id=CALCIUMPEROXIDE)
citations.finding: Listed for US food use as a dough conditioner / flour bleaching and maturing agent.
citations.simple: The US allows this to help strengthen and whiten flour for baking.

citations.ref: Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008, consolidated text 02008R1333 — EN — 16.12.2024 — 059.001 (EUR-Lex), Annex II Part B 'List of all additives' and Annex III
citations.finding: Checked against the consolidated primary text: 'E 930' occurs nowhere in the Union list — neither in Annex II Part B (the enumeration of all authorised additives) nor in Annex III. Under Article 4 the Union list is a positive list, so calcium peroxide has no authorised food use in the EU. Absence from the list is non-authorisation, not a ban or a withdrawal.
citations.simple: The EU does not allow this in food, because it is not on the approved list.

citations.finding: Butane, isobutane and propane are of low toxicological concern when used as food additives, with very low dietary exposure; 1,3-butadiene capped at ≤0.1% v/v in EU specifications.
citations.simple: Experts found this gas is of low concern in food, and people eat very little of it.
citations.source_title: Re‐evaluation of butane (E 943a), isobutane (E 943b) and propane (E 944) as food additives

citations.ref: Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 as amended by Commission Regulation (EU) 2017/874
citations.finding: Authorised as a propellant in vegetable oil pan spray (professional use only), water-based emulsion spray, and colour preparations at ≤1 mg/kg in food.
citations.simple: The EU only allows this gas as a spray propellant in a few products, with very small leftover amounts.

citations.ref: EFSA Journal 2025;23(1):9203 — doi:10.2903/j.efsa.2025.9203, Re-evaluation of butane (E 943a), isobutane (E 943b) and propane (E 944)
citations.finding: The three gases are of low toxicological concern as food additives with very low dietary exposure; EU specifications already limit 1,3-butadiene to ≤0.1% v/v; uncertainty remains about impurities not covered by current specifications.
citations.simple: Experts found this gas is of low concern in food, though some tiny impurities are not fully checked.
citations.source_title: Re‐evaluation of butane (E 943a), isobutane (E 943b) and propane (E 944) as food additives

citations.ref: Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 Annexes II/III as amended by Commission Regulation (EU) 2017/874
citations.finding: Permitted only as propellants in vegetable oil pan spray (professional use) and water-based emulsion spray at quantum satis, plus colour preparations at ≤1 mg/kg residue in food.
citations.simple: The EU only allows this gas as a spray propellant in a few products, with very small leftover amounts.

citations.finding: Re-evaluation established a new ADI of 15 mg/kg bw/day (NOAEL 1,500 mg/kg bw/day, UF 100), replacing the SCF's 9 mg/kg bw/day; concluded it is unlikely that acesulfame K intake is associated with cancer, glucose/insulin disturbance, cardiovascular risk or organ toxicity, and that neither the sweetener nor its degradation products raise genotoxicity concerns even at low pH and elevated temperature.
citations.simple: Experts reviewed this sweetener again and found it is unlikely to cause cancer or harm the body's cells.
citations.source_title: Re‐evaluation of acesulfame K (E 950) as food additive

citations.ref: EFSA Call for data on genotoxicity data on sweeteners, 2021-06-30 (efsa.europa.eu/en/call/call-data-genotoxicity-data-sweeteners)
citations.finding: E 950 had been listed as needing basic-battery genotoxicity testing (bacterial reverse mutation + in vitro micronucleus) — a gap that the completed 2025 re-evaluation closed.
citations.simple: Experts had wanted more cell safety tests on this sweetener, and the newest review covered that gap.

citations.ref: FDA, High-Intensity Sweeteners (fda.gov/food/food-additives-petitions/high-intensity-sweeteners)
citations.finding: Acesulfame potassium is one of six high-intensity sweeteners approved by FDA as a food additive, with an ADI established at pre-market review.
citations.simple: The US government has approved this sweetener for food and set a safe daily amount for it.

citations.ref: IARC Monographs Volume 134 (2023), aspartame; monographs.iarc.who.int/news-events/iarc-monographs-evaluation-of-the-carcinogenicity-of-aspartame-methyleugenol-and-isoeugenol/
citations.finding: A Working Group of 25 experts (Lyon, 6-13 June 2023) classified aspartame as Group 2B, possibly carcinogenic to humans, on limited evidence for an association with hepatocellular carcinoma in humans.
citations.simple: A group of experts said this sweetener may cause cancer, but the evidence is limited.

citations.finding: Full re-evaluation confirmed the ADI of 40 mg/kg bw/day and concluded aspartame was not of safety concern at current exposure estimates or at the ADI; intakes up to the ADI would not raise plasma phenylalanine above clinical guideline levels in normal subjects or PKU heterozygotes.
citations.simple: Experts reviewed this sweetener and found no health worry at the amounts people eat or the safe daily amount.
citations.source_title: Scientific Opinion on the re‐evaluation of aspartame (E 951) as a food additive

citations.ref: FDA, High-Intensity Sweeteners / Aspartame and Other Sweeteners in Food (fda.gov/food/food-additives-petitions/high-intensity-sweeteners)
citations.finding: Aspartame remains an approved US food additive; FDA states it has no safety concerns at approved conditions of use, while people with phenylketonuria should avoid or restrict it.
citations.simple: The US allows this sweetener and sees no safety worry, but people with PKU should avoid it.

additives.name: Cyclamic acid and its Na and Ca salts

citations.ref: 21 CFR 189.135 (govinfo CFR-2024-title21-vol3-sec189-135); order at 34 FR 17063, 1969-10-21
citations.finding: Food containing any added or detectable level of cyclamate is deemed adulterated in the US; the prohibition covers cyclohexane sulfamic acid and its calcium, sodium, magnesium and potassium salts.
citations.simple: The US does not allow this sweetener in food, and food containing any of it is treated as unsafe.

citations.ref: EFSA Call for data on genotoxicity data on sweeteners, 2021-06-30 (efsa.europa.eu/en/call/call-data-genotoxicity-data-sweeteners)
citations.finding: Cyclamates (E 952 i, ii, iii) are named as requiring in vivo follow-up because of POSITIVE in vitro genotoxicity results, plus testing of metabolites — an open, unresolved genotoxicity question, with no re-evaluation opinion published.
citations.simple: Some lab tests suggested this sweetener may harm the body's cells, and experts still have open questions about it.

citations.ref: European Commission amended proposal COM(2003) 277 final amending Directive 94/35/EC on sweeteners (EUR-Lex CELEX 52003PC0277)
citations.finding: Following the SCF opinion revising the cyclamate ADI (7 mg/kg bw/day, driven by cyclohexylamine toxicity), the Commission proposed cutting maximum permitted levels in soft drinks because 'there are indications that the ADI could be exceeded', soft drinks being a dominant intake route; levels were ultimately reduced to 250 mg/l.

citations.ref: EFSA Call for data on genotoxicity data on sweeteners, 2021-06-30 (efsa.europa.eu/en/call/call-data-genotoxicity-data-sweeteners)
citations.finding: Isomalt (E 953) is named among the sweeteners for which additional genotoxicity information was identified as needed — basic battery: bacterial reverse mutation (OECD TG 471) and in vitro micronucleus (OECD TG 487).

citations.ref: Europe PMC query of EFSA Journal for polyol re-evaluation opinions (executed 2026-08-10)
citations.finding: No EFSA re-evaluation opinion for isomalt exists; erythritol (E 968) remains the only completed polyol re-evaluation, so isomalt's EU status is still the pre-2009 SCF acceptance with no numerical ADI.

citations.finding: New ADI of 9 mg/kg bw/day as free imide (replacing the SCF's 5 mg/kg bw/day as sodium saccharin); P95 chronic exposure in the refined brand-loyal scenario was below the ADI; no genotoxicity concern for E 954 or its Remsen-Fahlberg-process impurities, BUT a concern for genotoxicity was identified for potential impurities associated with the Maumee process.
citations.simple: Experts set a new safe daily amount, but some impurities from one way of making it may harm cells.
citations.source_title: Re‐evaluation of saccharin and its sodium, potassium and calcium salts (E 954) as food additives

citations.ref: IARC Monographs Volume 73 (1999), 'Saccharin and its salts' (inchem.org/documents/iarc/vol73/73-19.html; IARC List of Classifications)
citations.finding: Saccharin and its salts were reclassified as Group 3, not classifiable as to carcinogenicity to humans, with inadequate evidence in experimental animals for the acid form — the rat bladder mechanism depends on rat-specific urine chemistry.

citations.ref: OEHHA notice, 'Saccharin Delisted Effective April 6, 2001 as Known to the State to Cause Cancer' (oehha.ca.gov/proposition-65/crnr/saccharin-delisted-effective-april-6-2001-known-state-cause-cancer)

citations.simple: California took this sweetener off its list of things known to cause cancer, after experts changed their view.

citations.finding: Re-evaluation concluded there is no need to revise the ADI of 15 mg/kg bw/day; exposure at currently authorised uses did not exceed the ADI in any population group (toddlers and children below ADI); no safety concern for genotoxicity of sucralose or its impurities, incl. sucralose-6-acetate at the 0.5% specification limit.
citations.simple: Experts checked this sweetener again and found people, including toddlers and children, eat less than the safe daily amount.
citations.source_title: Re‐evaluation of sucralose (E 955) as a food additive and evaluation of a new application on extension of use of sucralose (E 955) in fine bakery wares

citations.simple: Experts could not say it is safe in baked foods because very high heat may change it in unclear ways.

citations.finding: Sucralose-6-acetate (a manufacturing impurity and gut metabolite) was genotoxic in MultiFlow and in vitro micronucleus assays with a clastogenic mode of action; commercial sucralose samples contained up to 0.67% sucralose-6-acetate.

citations.simple: In lab tests, this sweetener harmed gut cells and gut germs, but this has not been shown in people.
citations.source_title: The artificial sweetener neotame negatively regulates the intestinal epithelium directly through T1R3-signaling and indirectly through pathogenic changes to model gut bacteria

citations.finding: Neotame is one of six high-intensity sweeteners approved by FDA as a food additive, with an ADI set at pre-market review.
